clips.title: What is command injection? - Web Security Academy
clips.why: PortSwigger, who teach web security for a living, show how text sent to a server becomes an operating system command: the attack from our story, from the attacker's side.
look: How input that is pasted into a shell command lets an attacker add a second command.
Characters such as ; and & that end one command and start another, like the semicolon in the poisoned step title.
clips.after: For Nova, the input is a step title or a ticket field instead of a web form, and the fix is the same: never hand that text to a shell.

clips.title: How to create a child process in nodejs (exec, execFile and spawn)
clips.why: A hands-on walk through execFile, the function the harness uses for every git call.
look: How execFile is given a file to run and its arguments as separate values, instead of one command line.
How the callback receives an error, stdout and stderr. In our code, promisify turns that callback into a promise you can await.
clips.after: The harness wraps exactly this in a one-line git() helper, so every git call passes an argument list.

clips.title: What is command injection? - Web Security Academy
clips.why: One minute on prevention, and it agrees with the lesson: do not call out to the shell with user input.
look: Their main advice: avoid calling operating system commands with input at all, and use safer interfaces.
Why escaping shell characters by hand is not the defence to rely on.
clips.after: execFile with an argument list is that safer interface in Node, and the platform uses nothing else.

clips.title: Node JS Tutorial for Beginners #13 - Streams and Buffers
clips.why: A gentle picture of streams for the Go deeper panel: data that arrives and is used in small pieces instead of all at once.
look: The idea of a stream: start using data before all of it has arrived.
Where Node uses streams: reading files and HTTP requests and responses.
clips.after: The gateway streams Claude's answers to Nova's machine this way, and the next lesson reads a request body as a stream.

practice.q: The harness must commit with a message built from a step title that the model wrote. Which call is safe?

options.why: The whole line goes through the shell, so a quote in the message ends it and a semicolon starts a new command.
No shell is involved. The message reaches git as exactly one argument, whatever characters it contains.
Removing single quotes leaves newlines and other shell tricks, and the string still goes through the shell.

practice.q: Finish the helper that every git call in the harness goes through.
practice.before:
const run = promisify(execFile);
const git = (...args: string[]) => run("git",
practice.hint: Pass the array itself, not a string made from it.
practice.why: Passing the array keeps every argument separate. Joining it into one string would bring the shell's rules back.

practice.q: await git("diff", "--cached", "--quiet") rejects, and error.code is 1. What does that mean?

options.why: git uses 128 for fatal errors, and a missing program gives "ENOENT". 1 here is an answer.

options.text: There are staged changes, so a commit makes sense
options.why: git diff --quiet answers with its exit code: 0 for no differences, 1 for differences.

options.text: The repository has no commits yet
options.why: That would be a fatal error with a message on stderr, not exit code 1.

practice.q: You run execFile("gti", ["status"]) by mistake. The promise rejects. What is error.code?
practice.hint: Error NO ENTry: the program was not found.
practice.why: When the program does not exist, there is no exit code at all. Node reports ENOENT, and the message says spawn gti ENOENT.

practice.q: Put the shell's reading of exec(`git commit -m "wip: ${title}"`) in order, for the title Add card"; touch HACKED; echo ".
items: The shell receives one string from Node
The quote in the title closes the commit message early
The semicolon ends the git command
touch HACKED runs as a second command
echo " turns the rest of the line into text to print
practice.why: The shell reads the string as instructions before any program starts, so text from outside becomes commands.
